catalog_quote: Assignment of stress in Punjabi is entirely predictable, yet it patterns differently in disyllabic and trisyllabic words. [p. 84] ... Punjabi exhibits a three-way distinction in syllable weight with monomoraic light syllables, bimoraic heavy syllables, and trimoraic superheavy syllables. [p. 84] ... In Punjabi, secondary stress is not found and main stress is not contrastive. ... Stress is also not affected by morphology. ... stress in Punjabi is distributed solely according to a pattern based on the weight of the syllables contained within a word. [p. 85] ... An exhaustive list of stress patterns for disyllabic words is shown in (4) and for trisyllabic words in (5). (4) ĹH pɛ́.laa 'before/earlier', H́H kán.daa 'thorn', ŚH dɔ́ɔl.naa 'to spill', ŚS áadʒ.kaal 'nowadays', LŚ bə.máaɽ 'sick', HŚ təɽ.búudʒ 'watermelon' (5) ĹLH tʃí.ʈi.aa 'letters', H́LH hóɽ.te.ɽaa 'odd', H́HS mə́ŋ.gɔl.vaaɽ 'Tuesday', ĹHS mí.ɽaa.kɔɔl 'near/next to me', HH́H bəkʰ.súu.wii 'safety pin', LH́H bɪ.ʃáa.naa 'to lay something down', LŚH bɪ.tʃáaɽ.naa 'to think', HŚH səŋ.gíit.naa 'to sing and dance' [pp. 85-86] ... the OT analysis reveals that Punjabi has a preference for stressing superheavy syllables, tends to avoid assigning stress to final positions ... foot construction occurs from right to left and stops once an appropriate foot has been detected that can bear stress—yielding stress placement on the leftmost foot [p. 92]

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (12 pp., text; also rendered pp. 85-86 as images because the text drops the acute accents). Each quoted fragment is present at the stated locator: p. 84 sec. 0 'Assignment of stress in Punjabi is entirely predictable, yet it patterns differently in disyllabic and trisyllabic words.' (verbatim); p. 85 'In Punjabi, secondary stress is not found and main stress is not contrastive.' and 'stress in Punjabi is distributed solely according to a pattern based on the weight of the syllables contained within a word.' (verbatim); p. 85 'An exhaustive list of stress patterns for disyllabic words is shown in (4) and for trisyllabic words in (5)'; exx. (4)-(5) on pp. 85-86 show exactly the pattern…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, non-contrastive single word stress with a three-way weight scale (L = CV, H = CVV/CVC, S = CVVC/CVCC). Disyllables: a superheavy syllable takes stress (the first if both are S; final stress only when the final is S and the initial is not); otherwise stress is initial (ĹH, H́H). Trisyllables: a final superheavy is skipped; stress the penult if it is heavy or superheavy (HH́H, LH́H, LŚH, HŚH), otherwise the antepenult (ĹLH, H́LH, H́HS, ĹHS). Analysed as moraic trochees built right-to-left with the leftmost foot stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: 'secondary stress is not found' (p. 85).
new_statements.exceptions: Dhillon: morphology (verb suffixes, plural) does not shift stress; rejects Arun 1961/Bhatia 1993 minimal pairs (galaa 'throat' vs galáa 'melt') as geminate-medial vs vowel-deleted monosyllables; notes Vijayakrishnan 2003 lists an HLŚ pattern unattested in his dialect. Other sources differ in detail: Bajaj 2019 (Malwai, p. 62) states penult default, ultima only if extra-heavy and penult not, antepenult if penult light (or all three heavy), reapplying after affixation; Tolstaya 1981/Kalra 1982/Bhatia 1993 (per Bajaj) report final stress on imperatives/causatives and on suffixes -vālā, -hār, -dār, -kār; Gill & Gleason 1962 describe the same facts as tone-onset placement on 1st vs 2nd syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level main stress in citation forms (di- and trisyllables; polysyllables not treated by Dhillon). Tone docks on the stressed syllable (Bailey 1914, Arun 1961, Bajaj 2019). Dialect: Majhi of villages near Amritsar, India.
new_statements.identity_note: Dhillon 2007 describes the Majhi dialect spoken in villages near Amritsar, India (the prestige basis of standard Eastern Panjabi, panj1256). Bajaj 2019 describes spoken Malwai (Malwa region, Indian Punjab), also under panj1256. Gill & Gleason 1962 and Arun 1961 describe literary/standard Indian Panjabi; Jain 1934 describes Ludhiani (Malwai/Powadhi border). Bashir & Conners 2019 (list of works to obtain) describe Lahore Panjabi, which is linguistically Majhi but is filed by ISO under Western Panjabi [pnb]; Hussain et al. 2020 describe Lyallpuri (Faisalabad, Pakistan).

new_statements.quote: Every monomorphemic word in Panjabi, except for unstressed clitics, carries lexical stress, which is realized through a combination of higher pitch, longer duration, and greater volume. Stress placement in monomorphemic words is largely predictable. It depends on the weight of a syllable and its position in the word. ... Stress is assigned to the penultimate (second to last) syllable, unless either (a) the ultimate (final) syllable is the heaviest, or (b) the antepenultimate (third from last) is heavier than the penultimate. ... [fn. 19] Stress is, however, not in itself contrastive in Panjabi.
new_statements.citation: Bashir, Elena & Thomas J. Conners. 2019. A Descriptive Grammar of Hindko, Panjabi, and Saraiki (Mouton-CASL Grammar Series 4). Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Sec. 3.4.1.3.2 'Stress in Panjabi', pp. 50-52.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.4.1.3.2 'Stress in Panjabi', p. 50 (rule + fn. 19), Table 3.17 'Summary of Panjabi stress placement' p. 51, p. 52 top (Shackle 2003: 592 caution); also sec. 3.4.1.2.2-3.4.1.3 pp. 48-49 (tone borne only by stressed syllables)

At p. 50 the three quoted stretches are on the page word for word: 'Every monomorphemic[18] word in Panjabi, except for unstressed clitics, carries lexical stress, which is realized through a combination of higher pitch, longer duration, and greater volume.[19] Stress placement in monomorphemic words is largely predictable. It depends on the weight of a syllable and its position in the word.'; 'Stress is assigned to the penul…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type and same placement algorithm as the catalog record (Dhillon 2007: weight-sensitive, three-way weight light/heavy/superheavy, main stress non-contrastive) -- the authors cite Dhillon 2007 for it. Adds: explicit default-penult formulation with the two override clauses (final if heaviest; antepenult if heavier than penult), geminates as VC.CV for weight, inherent stress on monosyllables, clitics unstressed, morphological exception for causative -ā stems, tone licensed only on stressed syllables, Shackle's caution that stress is not phonemic. No disagreement with Dhillon; silent on secondary stress for Panjabi where Dhillon says none.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lahore Panjabi: every monomorphemic word (clitics excepted) has one lexical stress; placement is predictable from syllable weight (three-way: light = short-V open, 1 mora; heavy = long V or short V + C, 2 morae; superheavy = long V + C(C), CC + long V(+C), or short V + CC, 3 morae) and position: default penult, but the final syllable is stressed if it is the heaviest in the word, and the antepenult is stressed if it is heavier than the penult (Table 3.17: H.H -> penult 'mālī, 'gājar; L.H / L.SH / H.SH -> final ba'cā, ma'kān, sal'wār; H.L.H -> antepenult 'pinjarā; H.H.H -> penult cam'kīlā). Geminates count as C.C (VC.CV) for weight. Monosyllables (non-clitic) are inherently stressed. Stress is not in itself contrastive (fn. 19); the near-minimal pair 'baccā 'child' / ba'cā 'save!' also differs in gemination, so 'as Shackle (2003: 592) cautions, it is problematic to consider stress to be phonemic in Panjabi' (p. 52). Stress interacts with tone: only stressed syllables bear high or low tone (pp. 49-50). Unstressed vowels adjacent to the stress reduce or elide (Urdu bāzār > Pj. bazār, savāl > svāl). Authors cite Bhatia (1993: 343), Malik (1995: 72, 79) and Dhillon (2007) for the placement rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress for Panjabi in sec. 3.4.1.3.2. (For Hindko/'Lahnda' the authors cite Varma 1936: 92 'only one primary word stress; secondary word stress is not found', p. 49; for Saraiki a secondary stress on the third syllable of initially-stressed trisyllables is noted, p. 52 -- neither statement is made for Panjabi.)
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed clitics carry no stress; compounds explicitly not treated (fn. 18); transitive/causative stems in -ā are regularly stressed on the stem-final /-ā/ (mar'vā.yā 'caused to be killed'), 'in most cases consistent with' the weight rule; placement is 'largely' (not entirely) predictable; borrowed words adapt by reducing/eliding pre-stress vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Lahore (Pakistani, Shahmukhi-written) variety of Panjabi (p. 47: 'the Lahore variety of Panjabi we describe here'); the catalog's Dhillon 2007 record is based on Indian (Doaba-area village) speakers. Both fall under panj1256. The same chapter also treats Hazara Hindko (3.4.1.3.1) and Saraiki (3.4.1.3.3, mostly initial stress per Shackle 1976) -- those statements belong to other glottocodes and were not used here.

tone_statements.quote: Punjabi is a contour tone language ... It is a tonal language with 5 tonal segments (i.e., p, k, t̪ , ʈ, ʧ) and three tones (i.e., high, low or level). ... When pitch is changing its position from maximum to minimum point it is be called falling or low tone. If pitch changes without showing any change then such type of tone is known as neutral or level tone. When pitch is changing its position from minimum to maximum point it is called rising or high tone (Singh, 2010). ... it has three segmental tones high /oˊ/, low /oˋ/ and mid tone /o̅ /
tone_statements.locator: p.47 Abstract and sec. 1 Introduction; p.50 sec. 2.2; p.51 sec. 2.4
tone_statements.summary: Calls Punjabi a contour tone language: three tones high(=rising), low(=falling), level/mid; PRAAT study of 6 Lahore speakers finds contours levelled. 'Tone is realized over two syllables.'.

tone_statements.quote: The end result of tonogenesis in Punjabi is a privative tonal system, in which the contrast is between lexical items that are specified for tone and those that are not (cf. Hyman 2001). ... Although the present study only found one phonemic tone in Punjabi, some authors claim a three-way tonal distinction ... only one phonemic tone is required in the phonological inventory. ... the data suggest that the basic structure of the tone is falling, perhaps High-Low for most speakers, but Mid-Low for speakers S2 and S4.

tone_statements.quote: Punjabi has three tones, with the falling and rising tones occurring due to the historically lost voiced aspirated consonants and word-final glottal fricative /ɦ/, and the default tone occurring elsewhere.

Argues Arun 1961/Bhatia 1993 'contrastive stress' pairs are mis-analysed.

sources.note: Ch. 4 reviews Kalra 1982 (rightmost non-final heavy, else leftmost), Malik 1995, Bahri 2011, Gargesh 1999, Singh 2004, Bhatia 1993; own acoustic study (duration, f0, amplitude; accented syllable = L*, lower f0, longer). Rules p. 62: monosyllables accented; disyllables penult unless ultima extra-heavy and penult not; trisyllables+ penult unless penult light and antepenult not, or all three heavy -> antepenult; reapplies after resyllabification.

sources.note: Second-hand: 'initial syllables usually carry stress in disyllabic nouns and adjectives [3]'; tone restricted to (usually stress-bearing) initial syllables.

sources.citation: Joshi, Shiv Sharma. 1978. The phonology of the verbal phrase in Punjabi (Doabi). PhD thesis, University of London (SOAS).
sources.note: Firthian prosodic study of verb words; stress marked and tied to tone exponency; notes causative stems have stress 'ultimate in disyllabic stems and penultimate in trisyllabic words' (e.g. [lebá] vs [lebána]); no general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Gill, Harjeet Singh & Henry A. Gleason Jr. 1962. A Reference Grammar of Panjabi. Hartford Studies in Linguistics 3. Hartford Seminary Foundation (ERIC ED013359).
sources.note: No 'stress' category; prominence handled as tone: every word has exactly one tone onset, on the 1st or 2nd syllable; 2nd-syllable onset when syll 1 has a centralized vowel, syll 2 a peripheral vowel and the intervening C is single (or /r ṛ n ɳ/), and in some tatsamas; otherwise initial (sec. 3.4 Tone Placement, pp. 48-50). Functionally a weight-conditioned accent-placement statement.

sources.citation: Dulai, Narinder K. & Omkar N. Koul. 1980. Punjabi Phonetic Reader. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
sources.note: Explicitly silent: foreword states word-stress and sentence-stress 'are not described'; only tone treated among suprasegmentals.

sources.citation: Arun, Vidya Bhaskar. 1961. A Comparative Phonology of Hindi and Panjabi. Ludhiana: Panjabi Sahitya Akademi.
sources.note: §59 (p. 36): 'Although stress is not a prominent feature of Panjabi, it is, however, sometimes phonemic' with pairs gala 'throat' / galá 'melt!' etc; §60: tone always falls on the stressed syllable; in trisyllabics the second syllable 'is invariably stressed'. No general placement algorithm.

sources.citation: Jain, Banarsi Das. 1934. A Phonology of Panjabi as spoken about Ludhiana and a Ludhiani Phonetic Reader. Lahore: University of the Panjab.
sources.note: Phonetic Reader §§83-84 (p. 166): Ludhiani has a 'pseudo-stress' (length+pitch, not force), illustrated by pairs 'tʌṛka vs taṛ'ka:, 'rala vs ra'la: etc; no placement rule. Historical part §182 (p. 94): accent shifted to the initial syllable except where a non-final syllable has a long vowel, then on the last such; §191: recent loans/tatsamas show penultimate accent.
